cultivar: Assamica-type clones and seedling bushes planted from 1929 onwards
processing: Mostly CTC and rotorvane black tea, withered, cut, fully oxidised and fired for tea bags and strong brewing; smaller lots of orthodox whole-leaf and broken grades are made for the loose-leaf range.
harvest_season: Plucked all year, every few weeks, in the equatorial highlands; there are no true seasons, though the drier months give slightly brighter tea.
appearance_dry: Small, dark, granular leaf in the CTC grades; neat black broken leaf with a few tips in the orthodox lots.
appearance_liquor: Bright reddish amber in the loose grades, deep and strong in CTC.
taste_profile: Light, brisk and clean with a mild maltiness and a gentle floral-grassy highland note, low in body and bitterness; built to take condensed milk in teh tarik without turning harsh.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, three to four minutes. For teh tarik, brew strong, add condensed milk and 'pull' it between two mugs until frothy. The orthodox loose grades are pleasant plain and lightly steeped.

vintage_note: Sold year-round by brand and grade (BOH's bags, 'Cameronian' loose leaf and estate-named tins), never by vintage; the bushes are plucked continuously and the factories blend across the year for consistency. Keeps a year or two sealed; it is an everyday tea, not a collector's one.
description:
The Cameron Highlands are a cool hill station in Pahang at 1,200 to 1,600 metres, and most of Malaysia's tea grows there (the rest comes mainly from Sabah, on Borneo). The industry is dominated by one company: BOH Plantations, founded in 1929 by the British-born businessman J.A. Russell as the first hill-country estate in Malaya, which still runs the Boh, Sungei Palas and Fairlie estates and whose tea bags are in every Malaysian kitchen. A second producer, Bharat, sells its Cameron Valley tea from the same hills and runs the roadside tea houses tourists stop at.

The tea is Assam-type leaf grown on steep terraced slopes, plucked year-round because the equator does not do seasons, and processed mostly by CTC for strength and consistency. That makes sense when you know what it is for: teh tarik, the pulled, frothed, condensed-milk tea that is Malaysia's national drink, and the kopitiam pot of strong tea with milk. A smaller orthodox range, sold loose and in gift tins, shows the leaf on its own terms.

Plain, it is a light, brisk, clean black tea with a touch of highland floral freshness and little bitterness; it is not a heavy Assam and does not try to be. With condensed milk it does exactly what it is supposed to. The orthodox lots, steeped shorter, make a pleasant plain afternoon cup, and the estates also sell green and flavoured teas aimed at visitors.

It is sold by brand and grade, year-round, with no vintage; BOH's standard bags and its 'Cameronian' loose leaf are the two things to know, and the Sungei Palas tea centre sells single-estate tins if you want to taste the hills themselves. Avoid buying it as a specialty tea at specialty prices; its virtue is that it is honest, cheap and consistent.

If you want to taste the region properly, make a teh tarik at home with it and then drink the same tea plain; the gap between the two is the whole story of Malaysian tea.
sources_note: Founding year 1929 and founder J.A. Russell are from memory. Bharat/Cameron Valley is mentioned as the second producer; its estate details are not given.
history:
Tea in the Cameron Highlands is tied to one company. BOH was founded in 1929 by J. A. Russell, a British-born businessman, in the middle of the Great Depression, and he took a land concession at Habu together with A. B. Milne, a veteran planter from Ceylon. The land was jungle on steep slopes, terraced with a steamroller and mule teams, and it became the first hill-country estate in British Malaya.

The name comes from the Bohea hills, the Wuyi range in Fujian. BOH is now Malaysia's largest black tea maker and its plantation the largest in the country, so for most Malaysians this tea simply is the everyday cup.
